In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Since the Bestower of gifts — in the universal cause that encompasses the seven invented things and the inventor of the seven — has gathered together in the noble divine Word (which is founded upon the knowledge of triads) the benefits and subtleties of meanings, and has ordained that the preamble and the rules of address in a book should begin with presenting the conditions of praise and with the opening of laudation — following the indication of the companion [of the Prophet], "Were it not for you" — and since He sent you as a mercy: "We have not sent you but as a mercy," the abode was adorned, and "We are the salt" struck the door of prophethood and the lands of grace; and He has laid down the path of guiding servants by removing deviation and enmity so that a wayfarer must travel — for every matter of worth, through the benefits set before the gate of considered opinion and companionship — the Bestower of gifts appears, and in the foundations of transmitted reports and the essentials of accounts, with clear reflection and holding fast to the firm rope: praise of the Necessarily Existent, the Bestower of favors and gifts, whose essence is beyond all description, whose attributes are without peer, whose equals are non-existent, transcendent above any straining of imagination or defining by tongues — sacred, beyond bodily form — and the opening of prefaces of knowledge begins herewith.

The wisdom and craftsmanship at the beginning of creation were bestowed upon the world in abundance, and among its kinds there is no compound, and it is called the simplest, and it is drawn from the elements and is as if it were nature itself. The pure simple takes on another form and has no nature, and it has no deficiency or combination. And the other, which has motion and nature, and whose elements are the purest of the second kind, is called compound, and the natural composites within it are among the most harmonious and balanced, and from the mixing of elements a new thing comes to be, and the celestial spheres and elements are shaped in the best form — and the best of forms is that which has been established, and thus the finest of forms governs the spheres and the elements. The four elements arranged together diminish to something, moving through degrees in multiples, just as the skin over the soft core is the most refined and temperate. The earth is the densest sphere, and the heaviest is that above it, and the celestial spheres with stars and planets are most elevated. In the Noble Scripture, mention of this is made frequently: "We have adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of stars, and as a guard against every rebellious devil" — the shooting stars go out to intercept them, and are enumerated. They are reckoned as blessed stars, some of them entering in a favorable way. A verse: the total is said to be one thousand and seven — the stars of al-Daybān — from the stars; the sun and moon are also called stars, and the sun is called the greatest luminary and the king of the planets, and it is the most magnificent in light and body, and the moon is called the smallest luminary. Five other stars are mentioned: they are held to cause love, fear, goodwill, and favorable fortune. The Arabs sometimes call them "the confined ones" and "the measured ones," or "the two neighbors," and some call them "the lucky stars." In the Noble Scripture, explicit mention of the soul and the moon appears frequently. As for the mention of the other planets, their bodies, and their mansions — all of this is established by Ptolemy, as he set it forth in his book the Almagest.

The statements of the ancient sages who came before, and of the servants and observers devoted to this science:

That several hundred and sixty-six times the cold and moist [humors] constitute the sphere of the Earth, according to the primary calculation among them — Saturn is [thus measured]. And roughly ninety-eight times cold and moist is the sphere of the Earth for Jupiter, and about eighty-two times is the sphere of the Earth for Mars, and about seventy-two and a half times the sphere of the Earth is for the Sun. Among these, the stars come in order from greatest to smallest. Among them, the one placed in the southern position has a form like a grain, and it measures about fifteen times the sphere of the Earth. Then each part measures one and a half times the sphere of the Earth for the ninth [sphere], and one part out of six of the Earth's sphere belongs to Mercury, and nine and a quarter parts of the sphere of Venus — that is what is said regarding Venus and the quarter of the orb — and it is greater than the ninth [sphere]. That measures one hundred and thirty parts of the sphere of the Earth, as is said, or from two thousand three hundred parts, as some say, and others say twenty thousand. In short, by agreement among the visible planets, all of them receive their illumination from the Sun, which has inherent luminosity, and from it the Sun gives off reflected light; the other luminous bodies vary in their brightness. If the sages declare that their illumination comes from their own inherent nature, they would argue: if it were truly so, when the Sun is eclipsed by the Moon, the Bull [Taurus] and the fire of the Bull would not appear — and if the greater luminary [the Sun] in this way were to descend to the lower regions, then certainly it would be clear proof that Venus and the benefic planets on the spheres from the first to the seventh: The First Sphere is the station of the Moon, and its proximity to the Moon and its movement and each of its aspects [is as follows:]

Bombay (Mambari), Sabar, and Bhindi Hund, and the one called Qatra Jumush — two thousand nine hundred farsakhs — and according to Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni], its distance from the equator is three hundred and thirty farsakhs and a half, by the measure of this diameter, as the authorities of Sindas have stated. And roughly three-sevenths of its diameter, and its circumference is two thousand and ten farsakhs. According to Abu Rayhan, its distance from the equator is [number] and six thousand and two [units]. Ninety-five farsakhs — and by the proof of the celestial sphere [number] — two [units], twenty-two, it is eighty-eight thousand two [units], and its elevation is determined as [number].

Sunba moves around and turns, traveling at a moderate pace, at thirteen degrees and four minutes and fourteen parts of the farsakhs. Some eight thousand four hundred farsakhs, and its elevation is [numbers given]. Although in speed it is swift in traversing distances of farsakhs — and the lower passage is only the sun, while the upper passages in cutting through farsakhs are faster than it — and the measure of the farsakhs of travel per hour will be revealed to you. The benefit to mankind corresponds to this: however many farsakhs the distance, it is greater, as Ptolemy and Hipparchus have stated — thirty-three thousand one hundred and sixty-two farsakhs — and they say its elevation is [number].

The second sphere is the station of Mercury, and among the Greeks, Romans, and Arabs it is known by various names. According to Abu Rayhan, the diameter of its orb is one hundred and forty-eight farsakhs and a quarter, and its circumference is four hundred and [number] farsakhs and a half, and its distance from the earth is [number] — six thousand four hundred and seventy farsakhs — and corresponding to this distance, the two orbs [follow below].

After [the calculation of the second sphere], the total comes to 1,362,388 farsakhs, four hundred and six thousand, three hundred and eighty-eight farsakhs. The elevation of the [sphere of] the Sun, because of its motion through the middle [course], and the measure of its arc as determined in the manner described, and eight daqiqas by this reckoning from the base of its breadth — a thousand and some hundred and three farsakhs — is its elevation, and the movement of its arrangement by the intermediate [calculation] is: 24,140 farsakhs is the elevation if there be a passage [of the sphere].

The Third Sphere is the pleasure-sphere of Venus. It is [known] by names among the non-Arabs, the Greeks, the Babylonians, the Byzantines, the Indians, and the Chaldeans. The diameter of its body, according to Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni], is 2,240 farsakhs, and its depth is 19 — two hundred and fifty-one — and a thousand and five hundred farsakhs, and so on. From the Earth, [it has been said,] 8,570,857 farsakhs, and seven farsakhs, as [the scholars] have stated. Its elevation, as reckoned by the distance of its sphere, is 11,514,100 — one thousand, one hundred and some — four hundred and fourteen farsakhs of elevation, and just as the middle course of Venus over sixteen days resembles that of the Sun, fifty-nine daqiqas and a fraction has been considered. By this reasoning, 197,318 farsakhs would be its elevation, and the middle [distance] of its sphere is: 12,198,111 — thousand thousand, five hundred thousand — one thousand and eighty-two farsakhs. Its elevation, as the middle [calculation] shows, is 199 — and the middle of the heavens.

And in the orbs, the soul is established in the body without cause — a resting place, as it were, for the King of the sky — the Fourth Sphere. Its stars are named [the Sun]: in Persian, Āftāb, Mihr, and Khurshīd; in Greek, Hēlios; among the Chaldeans, Nāran; in Roman, Helios; in Hebrew, Ḥā; in Indian, Hūr; and in Coptic, Bniyūkhwā. The diameter of its body, according to Abu Rayhan, is 11,193 — eleven thousand, nine hundred and thirty-six farsakhs — and by this reckoning, its circumference and body's circuit is 923,640 — forty thousand, four hundred and sixty farsakhs.

Three farsakhs, and after the equinox of Cancer, from the earth: 9, 13, 4, 8, 11 — thousands of thousands and two hundred and fifty thousand and eight hundred and ninety-nine farsakhs is its elevation, as has been established. From beyond, the revolution of its sphere: 5, 3, 18 — eight hundred thousand thousands and eight hundred and eighty-six thousand and three hundred and five farsakhs is its mean elevation; the first being 7, and so on. The Sun, at its mean motion, traverses each night and day the equivalent of fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds. The lowest point of the ecliptic is from this: 3, 9, 5, 1, 8, 2 — less than a thousand and some farsakhs, being ninety-three farsakhs in its elevation, as established. Each breath of a human being, in every exhalation — measured in farsakhs — and according to al-Tabari: 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 8, 1 — four thousand, eight thousand, four hundred farsakhs elevation and position. These are: 17, 7, 0 — and thus it constitutes the Fifth Sphere, the foremost of them. In Persian it is called Mihrām, in Turkish and Roman Arsh, and in Hebrew it is called Fitar. Its body, according to Abu Rayhan: 2, 8, 7, 1 — less than a thousand and seven hundred and ninety-two. And its two volumes: 7, 88 — five thousand farsakhs, plus seven farsakhs beyond. The equinox: 32, 32, 62 — two thousand thousands and two hundred and sixty-three thousands and three hundred and sixty-two farsakhs is its elevation, and accordingly the revolution of its sphere: 51, 28, 11, 7 — six hundred thousand thousand thousands and forty farsakhs and some, is its elevation in its first position, like the pouring of water. Mars, in a full day and night, is assigned such-and-such minutes; by this reckoning in general: 23 — three thousand and three hundred and sixteen farsakhs is its elevation. And none of the orbs of the planets, among those four, has motion, and those three are swift. No star among them is greater; according to al-Tabari: 2, 1, 32, 63, 4, 8, 7 — seven times a thousand...

One thousand and two hundred and fifty-six thousand, three hundred and eighty-two farsakhs is its elevation — meaning that which is cut off. I say: the Sixth Iwan is the Iwan of Jupiter. The Iranians call it Barjalis, and in the Nawruz and the Nawrumuz and the great and Roman nomenclature it is called Nuwambari. The diameter of the orb of Abu Rayhan is 1,988 — nine thousand eight hundred — eighty, and the distance in latitude is thirty-two thousand and fifty-four farsakhs. After the equinox from the nadir, according to 90, 99, 43 — nine hundred thousand thousand — one hundred and ninety thousand and four hundred and forty-three farsakhs is its elevation in total by calculation. And by the measure of Ibn, the revolution period of its sphere is 23, 53, 3 — two thousand — one thousand three hundred and fifty-three thousand and five hundred and thirty-five farsakhs, that being its elevation. And since the mean motion of Jupiter is five degrees per night and day, from this increase of 8, 9, 188 — one thousand eight hundred and ninety-five — its elevation becomes the mean of the orb. 79, 96, 79 — seven hundred thousand and two hundred — four thousand seven hundred and ninety-eight farsakhs for its elevation, that being its fifth. The Sixth Iwan: in Persian it is called Atazkawan, in Greek Afruqis, and in Hebrew Satarnakh. According to Abu Rayhan, its diameter is 2, 967 — nine hundred and sixty-seven thousand and three hundred farsakhs. And the distance from the equinox from the nadir is 24, 914, 14 — seven hundred thousand and one thousand and one hundred — fourteen thousand and two hundred and forty farsakhs for the planet, that being its elevation per calculation. The period of revolution of its sphere is one hundred and twelve hundred thousand and one hundred — three thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven farsakhs, that being its elevation. And since the mean motion of Saturn per night and day is two degrees, from this increase of 2, 2, 104 — ten thousand four hundred and twenty-two farsakhs — that is its elevation. [Final line:] the mid-line and mean-line.

Bīz al-Fakka: This is its figure. The scholars call it al-Fakka, and common people liken it to a bowl or cup-shape. It resembles a hand placed upon something, and its stars are in Libra and Scorpio. Its image stands with arms raised in agreement: [it appears] in the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth [degrees/positions].

Al-Ṣabāḥ: The meaning of this is that it was like Khusraw. A man is depicted standing on his feet with both arms stretched out, and his star is in Virgo. By agreement [of the authorities] it appears in the first, fourth, and fifth [positions]; and also in the third, fourth, fifth, and in the vicinity of the first. It is [the star] Simāk [Spica]: 2 [degrees] 4 minutes, 1 degree 10 minutes — al-Rāmiḥ [Arcturus]: 1 [degree].

The Jabi [a type of locust or creature]:
It is said that it resembles a man kneeling, and its stars are in Libra and Scorpio. It drives away [misfortune] without expenditure: [degree] 39, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth.

The Turtle:
That is to say, they [certain beings] devise stratagems and contrive [schemes], resembling [something]. They sought to conceal [the matter] and did not wish to reveal it. Its stars are in Capricorn. Its own image [brings protection] without expenditure: in the first, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth.

[Upper text]
The form of the hajj [pilgrimage bird] resembles the duck, stretching out its neck, and both wings raised, and it is also called the great bird. It is in Capricorn, Aquarius, with its ascensions in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in its form in the first, in the third, in the fifth, in the sixth, in the vicinity — in the measure of the fourth. 2

[Middle text]
The second: it resembles the one that settles upon its haunches like a camel, and its proportions are complete. It was sought that it is in resolution and uprightness, and every breath of its form with its ascensions upon the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, and in the sixth; a gathering rises from the hump.

All Persia and it is the first, the head of the Ghoul, a man on foot, the House, and desired.

The Great Dog — like a hound standing upright, in the degrees of [certain] mansions. By consensus: 29 [stars]. In the first [magnitude], in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth — in its image; in the first, in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth — around it, in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth.

It resembles a long serpent-fish, and its stars are like those of Aries, in the constellation of Cancer and Leo and Virgo. 9 6 2 7 1 4 2 1 — twelve thousand four hundred, twelve thousand seven hundred sixty and some farsakhs — this would be the captor of the outermost sphere. The Eighth Sphere is the dwelling-place of merit. It has been mentioned that the recorded fixed stars number from one thousand and twenty-two stars. Abu al-Husayn al-Sufi counted twenty-three stars more, and its explanation will follow in sequence. The smallness of the bodies of the fixed stars has been arranged in six ranks — the same ranks as the Greater Bear and its subdivisions: great, middle, small, lesser, minute, and dim — and the ranks have been assigned magnitudes. The very great ones are also called by the people of astronomy the noblest of stars. Whatever was said in the first and second magnitudes was agreed upon by all the astronomers as fifteen stars of the first magnitude. In the others there is disagreement among the scholars, and in this book the magnitudes are mentioned. Among the people of Samarkand, according to Abu Rayhan, and among many of the Indians, according to Abu al-Husayn al-Sufi, the author of the Book of the Constellations, we can count the number of stars — each magnitude explained in the figures, rendered in the form of depictions of the greatest among them. As for the fixed stars, their distances, even though among the weakest and smallest of the celestial bodies — every one of them is very small on earth but appears enormous to the eye — the observations that have been recorded, and the many small ones whose names and lords cannot be enumerated, God has made the people of astronomy call them hidden stars. For this reason the people of religious law do not accept astrological judgments as valid, and in various places the books of astrology on the idols of the Ka'ba are rejected as lies — because God Most High has not granted influence to the hidden stars, nor do the others have any influence either. And since no degree and no division of the celestial spheres can be firmly established, that is to say, their influences upon the influences of the recorded stars are foundational.

It did not happen, and those matters turned out contrary to imagination and expectation, and that false claim necessarily follows. And in the meaning of "Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us" — from this the truth of the matter becomes established, and that which appears in the form of fixed and hidden stars, other than the regulated planets, is none of those stars; rather, most of it is smoke that has been ignited and its temperature has caused the air to burn, so it appears luminous. And perhaps the planets are at a distance from the Earth of 12, 3, 3, 3, 22 — twenty-two — or more, thousands and three hundred and five hundred and a thousand and two parasangs, roughly. As for the ratios of the sizes of the planetary bodies relative to the Earth, according to the wise Ptolemy, by calculation of their diameters, and according to Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, there are differences in the calculations. Since in most books of the masters this figure was recorded in such a form, for the purpose of correction a change was made in it, and a line was drawn upon that sphere. Since beyond that sphere there is no planet, observation has not been possible beyond it. The eighth sphere, which is called the sphere of the fixed stars, has been described between the two poles of the great circle. As for its intrinsic motion, they say it does not accept motion from the ninth sphere, and the line of the ecliptic — called the line of the zodiac — is divided into twelve signs. Their names have been set forth by the great Farabi in verse in two lines: "We have raised the banner of nobility — Aries in exaltation and in the heights of sublimity / Death — like Gemini, Cancer, Leo / Virgo, the descent / Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces / And each degree attributed to minutes, and each minute to seconds, and each second to thirds — and twelve tenths have been measured, so that the variation may be reckoned and the origins known."

They record as a treasure, and the distance of the zodiacal belt according to Abu Rayhan Biruni is one hundred and nine farsakhs and a third and a twentieth of a daqiqa. Six thousand one hundred and forty-two farsakhs — three hundred and ninety-two — one thousand one hundred and twenty-three farsakhs; and the second part is eleven thousand seven hundred and seventy-five farsakhs, and the complete circuit of the twelve zodiacal signs, as thus enumerated, amounts to three hundred and seventy-seven thousand and some farsakhs; and in total three hundred and seventy-seven thousand, two hundred and fifty-five farsakhs in elevation.

The zodiac is divided from the ecliptic into two halves: one is called the northern half and one the southern half. The groupings of stars that Aristotle the sage — and some say seventy — set out in forty-eight figures, naming each one, so that knowledge of the positions of the stars, their sizes, lengths, breadths, and regions of the heavens might be obtained, are recorded in the running books. From those books the most authoritative accounts are now drawn.

And perhaps the sage Abu al-Muhsin made a summary of it, conforming to the year sixty-six of the Alexander era. From that time until now, when this book is being composed — the year one thousand and fifty-one — the Alexander era reckons four hundred and eighty-five years.

And also the sage Malaos, who came two hundred and forty-four years after him — corresponding to the twenty-fourth year of the Alexander era — composed works; and the book of the Almagest, which the sage Ptolemy after five [years]…

At the height of the year of compilation, eighty-eight, in the presence of a group of like-minded scholars, in a year corresponding to four hundred and fifty, during the reign of Shah Abu Dhu al-Arkan — although the foundation rests on the sayings of the ancient scholars who gave distinction to this art — and from the Islamic-era writings, the compositions of Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi, who flourished in the time of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid and likewise al-Ma'mun, calculated from the year of the conjunction: one thousand three hundred and thirty Alexandrian, every five and two hundred Hijri years, that is, seventy-nine and two hundred Yazdgirdi — the scholar Muhajja Jabir al-Stani al-Harafi, together with the scholars Khalid and others, including al-Akhtar, Mustakh, the science of Isa al-Istilaji, and others — compiled and composed works. Kushyar al-Jili and Masha'allah al-Misri also produced works thereafter. The Book of the Forms of the Constellations was likewise commissioned by al-Ma'mun: one hundred and forty-four dispatches in the year eight hundred and some, corresponding to two hundred and seventy-four Alexandrian years, equal to two hundred and fifty-four Hijri, two hundred and thirty-three Yazdgirdi — the scholar Abd al-Rahman, known as Abu al-Hasan al-Sufi, made it for Adud al-Dawla al-Daylami. Likewise the scholars of Egypt and Ibn A'lam of Baghdad thereafter, in the year one thousand and twenty-six Alexandrian, also produced works. The Qanun al-Mas'udi, made after the Book of Constellations by sixty-some years, in the year one thousand one hundred and forty-some Alexandrian, corresponding to the year four hundred and twenty-one, matching the year three hundred and twelve Yazdgirdi — the scholar Abu Rayhan Muhammad ibn Ahmad [al-Biruni], in service to Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna, produced it; and similarly a royal work thereafter — the service spanning one thousand four hundred and forty-some Alexandrian years, corresponding to five hundred and twenty-seven Hijri, and fifty-one Yazdgirdi — the scholar Husam al-Din...

The chief, by agreement of the physician and Halayn Abu Zari and the ascetic Abd al-Rahman the treasurer, constructed it. Niych Alabi carried out the work over twenty-eight years, in the year one thousand and seventy-two, corresponding to the year six hundred and fifty-five of the Hijra, and that is twenty-six years since the time of Yazdigerd. The physician Farid al-Din Abu al-Husayn Ali ibn Abd al-Karim al-Bakuyi continued it further for four hundred years, in the year one thousand six hundred and seventy-five, corresponding by the totality of three hundred and sixty-three of the Hijra, and three hundred and sixty-six of the Yazdigerd era. The trust of the sages was given to Khwaja Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Hasan al-Tusi, by the command of Hulagu Khan and Abqa Khan, together with Mu'ayyid al-Din al-'Urdi, Fakhr al-Din al-Maraghi, and Mukhir al-Din al-Akhlati, and Baha' al-Din, who built and arranged the observatory. From that time until now is seventy-five solar years. The circuits of Muhyi al-Din al-Maghribi were also constructed at that same time. Whatever small discrepancies were in the earlier tables, they were resolved, and so on in the same manner. The book contains much astronomical calculation, and a full account of it would be tedious. Therefore, from that source I have drawn upon what is useful, and between the lines of this book I have transmitted and recorded the forms, numbers, magnitudes, lengths, breadths, and names of the fixed stars as found in the book known as the Book of Fixed Stars, explained in a clear manner easy to follow and remember. Here I shall mention what has been recorded concerning the images and enumeration of the stars of the zodiacal constellations, established by observation, taken from the books without chain of transmission, for there are forty-eight figures of the stars. According to Abu Bakr, other than the small ones, Abu al-Husayn counts the small ones together: in the first magnitude, in the second magnitude, in the third magnitude, in the fourth magnitude, in the fifth magnitude — as described in the account.

Al-Su'ayra (a small star): According to Abu al-Husayn, together with al-Saghira, [it is] 2 in the first, in the second, in the third; in the fourth: Shakl; in the fifth: Leo (al-Asad); in the sixth.

Virgo (al-Sunbula): The image of a young woman, with a branch and grain in the lap of a man, seated and kneeling. The constellation of Virgo is called [such], in the first, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth; in the sixth; in her image, in the first; the second in the third, in the fourth; in the fifth; in the sixth; around it, the complete [stars]; al-Saghira in the fourth, in the fifth [partial]; al-Saghira Buskāniyya; her image in the first; in the third; in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth, in the fifth, in the sixth.
3 [hours] — 2 — 2

Libra: Since its name means "balance scale," it has the form of a man holding a scale upon himself. [Descriptions of its stars and their positions follow:] in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth [house/degree]. In its image, in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in its surroundings, third, in the fourth...

Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni] counted from the second and Abu al-Hasan counted from the third. Scorpio:

Since its name means "scorpion," [descriptions of positions follow:] in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth. In its image, in the second, in the third, in the fifth, in its surroundings, in the fourth... The third was counted by Abu al-Hasan [illegible] ... in the sixth.

Sagittarius: Since its image is current, its waist is in the form of a man from the navel upward...

By soul and constellation, this is the form of Sagittarius (al-Qaws), which is well known, and its stars in this figure are: in the third, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth.

Capricorn (al-Jadī): It is described as having neither fish nor goat fully, but is half goat and half fish, and its stars in this figure are: in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth.

Aquarius (al-Māʾ): The figure is that of a man pouring water, striking with his own foot, and this form is well known as Aquarius (Dalw), and its stars are: in the first, in the third, in the fourth, [illegible], in the first, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth, in the sixth.

The sixth, in its surroundings, the fourth star, Aquarius (al-Dalw).

Pisces: It is the form of two fish, with a cord connecting them at their tails. This figure, as it is well known, appears in the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth [climates], and in its surrounding fourth [region].

The figures of the remaining images in the northern regions — and according to Abu Rayhan, and according to Ibrahim — in the second, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth [climates], in their forms in the second, the first, the fourth, and the fifth [regions], in the sixth, in their forms in the second, the first, the third, the fourth, and the fifth [regions]. The northern figures of the Arabs agree in form in the first, the second, and the third [regions].

Its name is Taliha, and its stars are in Virgo; and as for the figure itself, by consensus it is in the fourth and fifth [houses/degrees].

The Crow (al-Ghurāb): its name means "crow," and its stars are in Virgo; and as for the figure itself, by consensus it is in the third, in the fourth, and it is in the fifth.

Quturus: The figure of a man down to the waist, in the shape of a horse without a head, belonging to the constellation of Taurus. Its stars are in Libra and Scorpio according to Abu Rayhan, and according to Abu al-Husayn: in the third, in the fourth, and in the fifth, in the sixth. Abu Husayn al-Sufi says this figure is well-known, and among these figures there are stars, and the number of its notable stars is one thousand and twenty-six.

God knows best.

Rijl al-Qaytus: It is the figure of a lion, and a man — Qaytrus — has taken hold of its leg and lifted it from the ground. Its stars are in Scorpio, and according to Abu Rayhan the number is such, and according to Abu al-Husayn: in the first, in the second, in the third, in the fourth, in the fifth. Abu al-Husayn says this figure is well-known and among its shapes there are six stars recorded.
